topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBECT404 - MICROCONTROLLERS & EMBEDDED SYSTEMS
> - **Module:** Module 1
> - **Topic:** Interrupts

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Interrupt:** An *interrupt* is an asynchronous event, either generated externally by a hardware peripheral/device or internally by the CPU itself, that temporarily halts the main program execution, forces the processor to save its current state, and transfers control to a dedicated routine called the **Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)** or **Interrupt Handler**. After the ISR completes, the processor restores its previous state and resumes the original program from the point where it was interrupted.

In the KTU 2024 Scheme syllabus context, the 8051 microcontroller family is the primary architectural reference, possessing **6 interrupt sources**:
1. **Reset** (highest priority, non-maskable)
2. **Two External Hardware Interrupts** (INT0, INT1)
3. **Two Timer Overflow Interrupts** (TF0, TF1)
4. **One Serial Port Interrupt** (TI/RI)

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy: The "Office Worker & Doorbell"

> [!NOTE]
> **Intuitive Analogy — The Busy Engineer:**
> Imagine a dedicated engineer engrossed in a complex design task at their desk. This is the **CPU executing the main program**.
> 
> *   **Without an interrupt (Polling method):** The engineer must stop work every few minutes, walk to the door, and *check* if someone is there. This wastes enormous time and breaks concentration — exactly like a CPU constantly checking a flag bit in a tight loop (`while(!flag);`).
> *   **With an interrupt:** The engineer simply installs a **doorbell**. When a visitor presses it, the bell *immediately* alerts the engineer. The engineer stops the current task (saves state in stack), answers the door (executes the **ISR**), and returns seamlessly to the design (resumes main program). This is the essence of **event-driven computing**.

### 1.3 Why Interrupts are Essential

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The core engineering rationale for interrupts is **efficiency, responsiveness, and real-time determinism**. The CPU spends **0%** of its time "looking" for events. Critical signals (e.g., emergency stop, data arrival) are serviced within a single machine cycle of detection, which is impossible with software polling loops.

| Mechanism | CPU Overhead | Response Time | Code Complexity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Polling (Loop)** | **High** (100% continuous checking) | Variable, often slow | Low |
| **Interrupt-Driven** | **Near Zero** (Hardware-triggered) | Deterministic & fast | Moderate |
| **Hybrid (Default Idle + Interrupt Wake-up)** | **Minimal** | Hardware-bound | High |

**Key Performance Metrics (Must Memorize):**
*   **Interrupt Latency:** Time delay from the moment an interrupt is *asserted* to the moment the *first instruction* of the ISR begins executing. Measured in **clock cycles**.
*   **Interrupt Response Time:** $\text{Latency} + \text{ISR Execution Time}$.
*   **Interrupt Recovery Time:** Time to restore context and return to the main program (typically 2 machine cycles in 8051).
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The Interrupt Processing Sequence (Operational Logic)

The 8051 handles an interrupt through a strict, hardware-implemented sequence. Let us decompose this into structured logical steps:

*   **Step 1 — Signal Assertion:** A peripheral or external pin sets a corresponding *interrupt request flag* (e.g., `IE0`, `TF0`, `TI`).
*   **Step 2 — Flag Sampling:** The CPU samples these flags at the **end of every machine cycle** (i.e., at S5P2 of the final cycle of the current instruction).
*   **Step 3 — Mask Verification:** The hardware checks the corresponding *enable bit* in the **IE (Interrupt Enable) SFR** AND the global enable bit **EA**. If any required bit is **0**, the request is ignored.
*   **Step 4 — Priority Arbitration:** If multiple requests occur simultaneously, the **IP (Interrupt Priority) register** and the *natural hardware priority* order resolve the conflict.
*   **Step 5 — Hardware Vectoring:** The CPU generates a `LCALL` to the predetermined **vector address** of the winning interrupt (e.g., `0003H` for INT0).
*   **Step 6 — Context Save:** Hardware pushes the 16-bit **Program Counter (PC)** onto the stack. *Note: 8051 does NOT automatically push PSW, ACC, or B; the ISR programmer must do this manually using `PUSH` instructions.*
*   **Step 7 — ISR Execution:** The CPU clears the interrupt flag (except for TI/RI, which must be cleared in software) and executes the ISR code.
*   **Step 8 — Return:** A `RETI` instruction pops PC from the stack, restoring execution. `RETI` *also* informs the interrupt controller that the ISR is complete, allowing further interrupts of the *same or lower* priority.

> [!NOTE]
> **Critical Distinction for 8051:**
> `RETI` (Return from Interrupt) and `RET` (Return from subroutine) are **not interchangeable**. `RETI` is mandatory because it signals the hardware priority logic. Using `RET` inside an ISR breaks the entire interrupt priority system.

### 2.2 Classification of Interrupts (Exam Favorite Topic)

| Classification Type | Definition | 8051 Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hardware Interrupt** | Triggered by an external electrical signal on a pin. | INT0 (P3.2), INT1 (P3.3) |
| **Software Interrupt** | Triggered by an internal CPU condition. | Timer overflow, Serial byte received |
| **Maskable Interrupt** | Can be disabled (masked) by a control bit. | All 8051 interrupts *except Reset* |
| **Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI)** | Cannot be disabled; serviced always. | **Reset** |
| **Vectored Interrupt** | Has a fixed, dedicated memory address. | All 8051 interrupts |
| **Edge-Triggered** | Activated on a falling/rising edge (8051 default). | INT0/INT1 when `ITx = 1` |
| **Level-Triggered** | Activated on a logic low level. | INT0/INT1 when `ITx = 0` |

### 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet & SFR Map (High-Yield Cheat Sheet)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The following table contains all mathematically verifiable formulas and key register values required for solving KTU examination problems. Constants like clock frequency $f_{\text{osc}} = 11.0592 \text{ MHz}$ are standard because they generate exact integer baud rates (e.g., **9600 baud**).

| Parameter | Formula / Register Value | Units | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Machine Cycle Duration | $T_{\text{mc}} = \dfrac{12}{f_{\text{osc}}}$ | seconds (s) | 8051 uses 12 clocks per cycle |
| Interrupt Latency (8051) | $L = (2 \text{ to } 8) \cdot T_{\text{mc}} + 2 \cdot T_{\text{mc}}$ | seconds (s) | 2–8 cycles for current instruction, 2 cycles for `LCALL` |
| Interrupt Vector Spacing | $\Delta_{\text{vec}} = 8$ | bytes | Each ISR has 8 bytes of reserved space |
| Timer Reload Value (Mode 1, 16-bit) | $\text{THx TLx} = 65536 - (f_{\text{osc}} \cdot t_{\text{delay}}) / 12$ | decimal | Used when timer overflow ISR fires |
| TH0/TH1 Upper Byte | $H = \lfloor (65536 - N) / 256 \rfloor$ | integer | For 16-bit timer interrupts |
| TL0/TL1 Lower Byte | $L = (65536 - N) \mod 256$ | integer | For 16-bit timer interrupts |
| EA (Global Enable) | Address **0xA8**, Bit **7** | bit | Must be 1 to enable any maskable int |
| IE SFR Address | **0xA8** (Bit-addressable) | byte | EA, ES, ET1, EX1, ET0, EX0 |
| IP SFR Address | **0xB8** (Bit-addressable) | byte | PS, PT1, PX1, PT0, PX0 |
| TCON (Int Control) | **0x88** (Bit-addressable) | byte | IT0, IE0, IT1, IE1, TR0, TF0, TR1, TF1 |

### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

> [!NOTE]
> Interrupts are the **backbone of all real-time embedded systems**. Practical applications include:
> *   **Automotive Airbag Systems:** A crash sensor triggers a hardware interrupt; the ISR deploys airbags within **microseconds** — polling would be fatal.
> *   **Industrial PLCs:** External interrupts detect emergency-stop button presses, halting machinery instantly.
> *   **IoT Edge Devices:** UART receive interrupts free the CPU from waiting for sensor data, allowing it to enter low-power sleep modes, conserving battery life.
> *   **Medical Heart Pacemakers:** Timer overflow interrupts generate precise pulse timing with $\mu$s accuracy.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Exhaustive Derivation: Interrupt Latency Calculation

This derivation calculates the **worst-case interrupt response time** — a frequent KTU question worth 7 marks.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Problem Statement:**
> An 8051 system uses a crystal frequency $f_{\text{osc}} = 11.0592 \text{ MHz}$. Calculate the worst-case interrupt latency for an external interrupt INT0, given that the longest instruction (`MUL AB`) is currently executing when INT0 is asserted.

**Step 1 — Calculate the Machine Cycle Period**

The 8051 divides the oscillator frequency by **12** to produce the machine cycle clock.

$$T_{\text{mc}} = \frac{12}{f_{\text{osc}}}$$

Substituting $f_{\text{osc}} = 11.0592 \times 10^6 \text{ Hz}$:

$$T_{\text{mc}} = \frac{12}{11.0592 \times 10^6}$$

$$T_{\text{mc}} = 1.085 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s}$$

$$T_{\text{mc}} = 1.085 \text{ } \mu\text{s}$$

**Step 2 — Identify the Longest Instruction Cycle Count**

From the 8051 instruction set reference, `MUL AB` is a **4-machine-cycle** instruction (4 × $T_{\text{mc}}$), making it one of the longest. We take this as the worst-case delay before the CPU can sample the interrupt flag.

$$T_{\text{worst-instr}} = 4 \cdot T_{\text{mc}} = 4 \cdot 1.085 \text{ } \mu\text{s} = 4.34 \text{ } \mu\text{s}$$

**Step 3 — Add the Internal LCALL Cycle**

Once the flag is sampled, the 8051 hardware automatically executes an internal `LCALL` to the vector address, which consumes **2 machine cycles**.

$$T_{\text{lcall}} = 2 \cdot T_{\text{mc}} = 2 \cdot 1.085 \text{ } \mu\text{s} = 2.17 \text{ } \mu\text{s}$$

**Step 4 — Total Worst-Case Latency Formula**

The general formula for the worst-case interrupt latency is:

$$L_{\text{worst}} = (N_{\text{cycles}} \cdot T_{\text{mc}}) + (2 \cdot T_{\text{mc}})$$

Where $N_{\text{cycles}}$ is the cycle count of the currently executing instruction. Substituting our values:

$$L_{\text{worst}} = (4 \cdot T_{\text{mc}}) + (2 \cdot T_{\text{mc}})$$

$$L_{\text{worst}} = 6 \cdot T_{\text{mc}} = 6 \cdot 1.085 \text{ } \mu\text{s}$$

$$\boxed{L_{\text{worst}} = 6.51 \text{ } \mu\text{s}}$$

### 3.2 Exhaustive Derivation: Timer Reload Value for Periodic Interrupts

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Problem Statement:**
> Configure Timer 0 in Mode 1 (16-bit) to generate an interrupt every **50 ms** using $f_{\text{osc}} = 11.0592 \text{ MHz}$. Calculate the TH0 and TL0 reload values.

**Step 1 — Compute the Number of Timer Counts Required**

Each timer tick occurs every machine cycle ($T_{\text{mc}} = 1.085 \text{ } \mu\text{s}$ from above). The required number of timer increments $N$ is:

$$N = \frac{t_{\text{delay}}}{T_{\text{mc}}}$$

$$N = \frac{50 \times 10^{-3}}{1.085 \times 10^{-6}}$$

$$N = 46,082.95 \approx 46,083 \text{ counts}$$

**Step 2 — Compute the 16-bit Reload Value**

In Mode 1, the timer is 16-bit and overflows from `0xFFFF` to `0x0000`. The starting value to be loaded is:

$$N_{\text{reload}} = 65{,}536 - N$$

$$N_{\text{reload}} = 65{,}536 - 46{,}083$$

$$N_{\text{reload}} = 19{,}453$$

Converting $19{,}453$ to hexadecimal:

$$19{,}453 \div 256 = 75.99 \quad \Rightarrow \quad H = 75_{10} = 0x4B$$

$$19{,}453 \mod 256 = 253_{10} = 0xFD$$

Therefore:

$$\boxed{\text{TH0} = 0x4B, \quad \text{TL0} = 0xFD}}$$

**Step 3 — Verification**

We verify the delay: Timer counts up by $46{,}083$, taking $46{,}083 \times 1.085 \text{ } \mu\text{s} = 49.99 \text{ ms} \approx 50 \text{ ms}$. ✔

### 3.3 Analytical Matrix: Natural Hardware Priority Order

The 8051 has a fixed, hardware-implemented priority order. The following matrix is the **definitive KTU exam reference**:

| Priority Rank | Interrupt Source | Flag Bit | Vector Address (Hex) | IE Enable Bit | IP Priority Bit |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1 (Highest)** | **Reset** | — | **0x0000** | Always Enabled | Non-maskable |
| **2** | External Interrupt 0 (INT0) | IE0 | **0x0003** | EX0 | PX0 |
| **3** | Timer 0 Overflow | TF0 | **0x000B** | ET0 | PT0 |
| **4** | External Interrupt 1 (INT1) | IE1 | **0x0013** | EX1 | PX1 |
| **5** | Timer 1 Overflow | TF1 | **0x001B** | ET1 | PT1 |
| **6 (Lowest)** | Serial Port (TX/RX) | TI/RI | **0x0023** | ES | PS |

> [!NOTE]
> If two interrupts have the **same** IP priority level, the natural hardware order above applies. If `IP` bits differ, the one with `IP = 1` wins. This is a **2-tier priority system**.
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Mermaid Diagram: The Interrupt Handling Lifecycle

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[CPU Executes Main Program] --> B{Interrupt Flag Set?}
    B -- No --> A
    B -- Yes --> C{IE Enable Bit Set AND EA = 1?}
    C -- No --> A
    C -- Yes --> D{Priority Check: Multiple Requests?}
    D -- Single Request --> F[Hardware generates LCALL to Vector Address]
    D -- Multiple Requests --> E[Resolve via IP Register and Natural Priority]
    E --> F
    F --> G[Push 16-bit PC onto Stack]
    G --> H[Clear Interrupt Flag automatically]
    H --> I[Execute Interrupt Service Routine ISR]
    I --> J{RETI Instruction Encountered?}
    J -- No --> I
    J -- Yes --> K[Pop PC from Stack via RETI]
    K --> L[Resume Main Program from Saved PC]
    L --> A
```

### 4.2 Mermaid Diagram: 8051 Interrupt Source Architecture Block

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph INTERNAL[Internal Sources]
        T0[Timer 0 Overflow]
        T1[Timer 1 Overflow]
        SP[Serial Port TI or RI]
    end

    subgraph EXTERNAL[External Hardware Sources]
        E0[INT0 Pin P3.2]
        E1[INT1 Pin P3.3]
        RS[RESET Pin P3.0 - Highest Priority]
    end

    subgraph CONTROL[Control Logic Layer]
        TCON[TCON Register - Edge Level]
        IE[IE Register at 0xA8 - Enable Mask]
        IP[IP Register at 0xB8 - Priority]
    end

    subgraph CPU[CPU Response]
        ARB[Priority Arbiter]
        VEC[Vector Generator]
        ISR[Interrupt Service Routine]
    end

    T0 --> ARB
    T1 --> ARB
    SP --> ARB
    E0 --> ARB
    E1 --> ARB
    RS --> ARB
    TCON --> E0
    TCON --> E1
    IE --> ARB
    IP --> ARB
    ARB --> VEC
    VEC --> ISR
```

### 4.3 Mermaid Diagram: Interrupt Vector Memory Map

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M0000[0x0000 - RESET Vector]:::hi
    M0003[0x0003 - INT0 ISR Slot - 8 bytes]
    M000B[0x000B - Timer 0 ISR Slot - 8 bytes]
    M0013[0x0013 - INT1 ISR Slot - 8 bytes]
    M001B[0x001B - Timer 1 ISR Slot - 8 bytes]
    M0023[0x0023 - Serial Port ISR Slot - 8 bytes]
    M0030[0x0030 onwards - User Main Program]:::endnode

    M0000 --> M0003 --> M000B --> M0013 --> M001B --> M0023 --> M0030

    classDef hi fill:#FFD700,stroke:#B8860B,stroke-width:2px,color:#000
    classDef endnode fill:#90EE90,stroke:#006400,stroke-width:2px,color:#000
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Insight:** Since each interrupt vector is only **8 bytes** apart, complex ISRs (e.g., for the serial port) typically place a short `LJMP` or `AJMP` at the vector address, redirecting execution to a larger routine located elsewhere in code memory.
<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### Part A: Short-Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

**Q1. [KTU University Exam - May 2023]**
*Define the term "Interrupt Latency" and list the factors that affect it in the 8051 microcontroller.*

> [!NOTE]
> **Model Answer (3 Marks):**
> **Interrupt Latency** is the time delay between the assertion of an interrupt request signal and the execution of the *first instruction* of the corresponding Interrupt Service Routine (ISR).
> 
> **Factors affecting latency in 8051:**
> 1.  The cycle count of the instruction currently executing when the interrupt is asserted (longest is 4 cycles for `MUL AB`/`DIV AB`).
> 2.  The 2-machine-cycle overhead of the internal `LCALL` to the vector address.
> 3.  Whether the interrupt is masked (`EA = 0` → infinite latency) or disabled.
> 4.  The clock oscillator frequency $f_{\text{osc}}$, since $T_{\text{mc}} = 12 / f_{\text{osc}}$.
> 
> **Formula:** $L_{\text{max}} = (N_{\text{max cycles}} + 2) \cdot T_{\text{mc}}$

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam - Dec 2022]**
*Differentiate between Level-Triggered and Edge-Triggered external interrupts in 8051. Which bit controls this behavior?*

> [!NOTE]
> **Model Answer (3 Marks):**
> 
> | Aspect | Level-Triggered | Edge-Triggered |
> | :--- | :--- | :--- |
> | Activation | Low logic level (0V) on INTx pin | Falling edge (High→Low transition) |
> | Flag (IEx) | Set only while pin is LOW | Latched on the edge, must be cleared in software |
> | Re-triggering | Multiple interrupts if pin stays LOW | Only one interrupt per edge |
> | Use Case | Wired-OR interrupt sharing | Clean pulse signals |
> 
> **Control Bit:** The **`IT0`** (for INT0) and **`IT1`** (for INT1) bits in the **TCON** register at address **0x88** control this. **`ITx = 0`** → Level-Triggered. **`ITx = 1`** → Edge-Triggered (Falling edge).

---

### Part B: 14-Mark Questions with Internal Choice

---

## ❓ CHOICE QUESTION A (14 Marks)

**Q3. [KTU University Exam - June 2024 Model Paper]**
**(a)** With a neat block diagram, explain the interrupt structure of the 8051 microcontroller. List all interrupt sources with their vector addresses and default priority order. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** An 8051 system uses an 11.0592 MHz crystal. Timer 0 is configured in Mode 1 to generate an interrupt every 25 ms. Calculate the values to be loaded into **TH0** and **TL0**, and write the complete 8051 assembly program to flash an LED connected to **P1.0** upon each overflow. **(7 Marks)**

### ✅ Model Solution for Q3(a):

The 8051 has 6 interrupt sources, divided into three categories:

**1. External Interrupts (Hardware-triggered):**
*   **INT0** (P3.2): Vector `0x0003`
*   **INT1** (P3.3): Vector `0x0013`

**2. Internal Timer Interrupts:**
*   **TF0** (Timer 0 Overflow): Vector `0x000B`
*   **TF1** (Timer 1 Overflow): Vector `0x001B`

**3. Serial Communication Interrupt:**
*   **TI/RI** (Transmit/Receive): Vector `0x0023`

**Priority Order (Highest to Lowest):**

$$\text{Reset} > \text{INT0} > \text{TF0} > \text{INT1} > \text{TF1} > \text{Serial Port}$$

**Key SFRs:**
*   `IE` (0xA8): `EA`, `ET2`, `ES`, `ET1`, `EX1`, `ET0`, `EX0` — Enable bits.
*   `IP` (0xB8): `PS`, `PT2`, `PT1`, `PX1`, `PT0`, `PX0` — Priority bits.
*   `TCON` (0x88): `IT1`, `IE1`, `IT0`, `IE0` — Trigger type for external ints.

### ✅ Model Solution for Q3(b):

**Step 1 — Calculate Machine Cycle Period:**

$$T_{\text{mc}} = \frac{12}{11.0592 \times 10^6} = 1.085 \text{ } \mu\text{s}$$

**Step 2 — Calculate Required Timer Counts for 25 ms:**

$$N = \frac{25 \times 10^{-3}}{1.085 \times 10^{-6}} = 23{,}041 \text{ counts}$$

**Step 3 — Calculate 16-bit Reload Value:**

$$N_{\text{reload}} = 65{,}536 - 23{,}041 = 42{,}495$$

Converting to hex:
$$42{,}495 = 0xA5FF \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{TH0} = 0xA5, \quad \text{TL0} = 0xFF}$$

**Step 4 — Complete Assembly Program:**

```assembly
        ORG 0000H
        LJMP MAIN
        ORG 000BH          ; Timer 0 ISR Vector
        LJMP TIMER0_ISR

        ORG 0030H
MAIN:   MOV TMOD, #01H    ; Timer 0, Mode 1 (16-bit)
        MOV TH0, #0A5H    ; Load high byte
        MOV TL0, #0FFH    ; Load low byte
        SETB ET0           ; Enable Timer 0 interrupt
        SETB EA            ; Enable global interrupts
        SETB TR0           ; Start Timer 0
HERE:   SJMP HERE          ; Idle loop, wait for interrupts

TIMER0_ISR:
        MOV TH0, #0A5H    ; Reload for next 25 ms
        MOV TL0, #0FFH
        CPL P1.0           ; Toggle LED
        RETI
        END
```

---

## ❓ CHOICE QUESTION B (14 Marks)

**Q4. [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]**
**(a)** Explain the function of the **IE** (Interrupt Enable) and **IP** (Interrupt Priority) Special Function Registers in the 8051. Show the bit format and describe what happens when two interrupts are asserted simultaneously. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** What is the difference between a **maskable** and **non-maskable** interrupt? With a suitable example, explain how the 8051 handles a **nested interrupt** when a higher-priority event occurs during the execution of a lower-priority ISR. **(7 Marks)**

### ✅ Model Solution for Q4(a):

**IE Register (Address 0xA8 — Bit Addressable):**

| Bit | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Name | **EA** | — | — | **ES** | **ET1** | **EX1** | **ET0** | **EX0** |

*   **`EA` (Enable All):** Global master switch. Must be 1 for any interrupt to be recognized.
*   **`ES`:** Enables serial port interrupt (`TI`/`RI`).
*   **`ET1`/`ET0`:** Enable Timer 1 / Timer 0 overflow interrupts.
*   **`EX1`/`EX0`:** Enable External Interrupts INT1 / INT0.

**IP Register (Address 0xB8 — Bit Addressable):**

| Bit | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Name | — | — | — | **PS** | **PT1** | **PX1** | **PT0** | **PX0** |

*   **`P? = 1`:** Sets the interrupt to **High Priority**.
*   **`P? = 0`:** Sets the interrupt to **Low Priority** (default).

**Simultaneous Interrupts:**
The 8051 uses a **2-tier priority system**:
1.  **Tier 1:** Compare IP register bits. The interrupt with `P? = 1` wins.
2.  **Tier 2 (Tie-breaker):** If both are at the same IP level, the **natural hardware priority** (Reset > INT0 > TF0 > INT1 > TF1 > Serial) decides the winner.

### ✅ Model Solution for Q4(b):

**Maskable vs Non-Maskable:**

| Feature | Maskable Interrupt | Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Can be disabled? | Yes, via `IE` register bits | **No** — always serviced |
| 8051 Example | All except Reset | **Reset** (RST pin) |
| Use Case | Peripheral events, timers | Critical failures, system initialization |

**Nested Interrupt Handling Example:**

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Scenario:** The 8051 is currently executing the **Timer 0 ISR** (low priority, `PT0 = 0`) when a **Serial Port interrupt** arrives with high priority (`PS = 1`).

**Step-by-step behavior:**
1.  CPU enters Timer 0 ISR, pushes PC onto stack.
2.  Serial Port interrupt is asserted; hardware checks `PS = 1` (high) vs `PT0 = 0` (low).
3.  Since Serial has higher priority, CPU **interrupts the current ISR** (this is **nesting**).
4.  Hardware pushes the *current* PC (which was executing the Timer 0 ISR) onto the stack again.
5.  CPU jumps to vector `0x0023` and executes the Serial ISR.
6.  When Serial ISR finishes, the `RETI` instruction pops the older PC, resuming Timer 0 ISR *from exactly where it was paused*.
7.  Timer 0 ISR's `RETI` then returns to the main program.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls (Marks Lost Here!):**
> 1.  **Forgetting the IE register:** Many students enable `ET0` but forget to set `EA = 1`. The interrupt will never fire. This is the **#1 reason** students get zero in lab vivas.
> 2.  **Confusing `RETI` with `RET`:** A `RET` instruction does *not* inform the interrupt controller. The priority logic remains "busy," and lower-priority interrupts will be **permanently locked out**. Always use `RETI`.
> 3.  **Not clearing TI/RI flags:** Unlike timer and external interrupts, the 8051 does *not* auto-clear the serial flags. Forgetting `CLR TI` and `CLR RI` causes an infinite interrupt loop that hangs the CPU.
> 4.  **Forgetting to reload Timer registers:** In Mode 1, TH0/TL0 reset to 0 after overflow. The ISR **must** reload them, or the next delay will be wrong (defaulting to 65,536 × 1.085 µs ≈ 71 ms).
> 5.  **Wrong vector address:** Common mistake is putting the ISR at `0x0000` (Reset vector) instead of `0x000B` (Timer 0). The CPU will execute the *wrong* code upon overflow.

---

### 📌 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Module 1: Interrupts**
> 
> *   **Six 8051 Interrupt Sources:** Reset, INT0, TF0, INT1, TF1, Serial (TI/RI).
> *   **Vector Addresses:** `0000H`, `0003H`, `000BH`, `0013H`, `001B`, `0023H` — each spaced **8 bytes** apart.
> *   **Two Essential SFRs:** `IE` (`0xA8`) for enabling, `IP` (`0xB8`) for prioritizing.
> *   **Global Switch:** `EA` must be 1; else no maskable interrupt works.
> *   **Trigger Control:** `IT0`/`IT1` in TCON — 0 = Level Low, 1 = Falling Edge.
> *   **Natural Priority:** Reset > INT0 > TF0 > INT1 > TF1 > Serial.
> *   **Machine Cycle:** $T_{\text{mc}} = 12 / f_{\text{osc}}$. With **11.0592 MHz**, $T_{\text{mc}} = 1.085 \text{ } \mu\text{s}$.
> *   **Latency Formula:** $L_{\text{max}} = (N_{\text{cycles}} + 2) \cdot T_{\text{mc}}$, max $N_{\text{cycles}} = 4$.
> *   **Timer Reload (Mode 1):** $N_{\text{reload}} = 65{,}536 - (t_{\text{delay}} / T_{\text{mc}})$.
> *   **Return Instruction:** Always use **`RETI`**, never `RET`, inside an ISR.
> *   **Auto-cleared Flags:** IE0, IE1, TF0, TF1 are cleared by hardware.
> *   **Software-cleared Flags:** **TI** and **RI** must be cleared manually in the ISR.
> *   **Context Save:** 8051 only pushes PC automatically; preserve ACC, B, PSW manually with `PUSH`/`POP`.
> *   **Nesting Rule:** A high-priority ISR can preempt a low-priority ISR, but **not vice versa**. Same-priority interrupts cannot preempt each other.

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PBECT404 - MICROCONTROLLERS & EMBEDDED SYSTEMS > - **Module:** Module 4 > - **Topic:** Serial Port Programming - Transmitting and Receiving # 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology) The **8051 Serial Port** is an on-chip **Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter (UART)** peripheral that enables full-duplex, asynchronous, frame-based serial communication between the microcontroller and external devices. It uses two dedicated Special Function Registers (SFRs) — the **SBUF (Serial Buffer)** register and the **SCON (Serial Control)** register — and is clocked by **Timer 1** in its **8-bit auto-reload (Mode 2)** configuration to generate the precise **baud rate** required for serial data exchange. > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight (Module 4):** > Serial Port Programming covers the hardware-level programming of the 8051's built-in UART, including SCON configuration, Timer-1 based baud rate generation, character transmission by writing to SBUF, and character reception by reading from SBUF with flag-based polling or interrupt-driven mechanisms. ## 1.2 Intuitive Real-World Analogy Imagine the **8051 microcontroller as a post office clerk** with two separate mail slots: - A **green "OUT" slot** (the *Transmit SBUF*) — anything dropped into this slot is automatically stamped with a start bit, the 8 data bits (least significant bit first), and a stop bit, and then transmitted one bit at a time over a single wire (TxD pin P3.1) at a fixed, agreed-upon speed (the *baud rate*). - A **red "IN" slot** (the *Receive SBUF*) — when a properly formatted serial frame arrives on the RxD pin (P3.0), the 8 data bits are automatically assembled and dropped into this slot, ringing a small bell (the *RI flag*) to alert the CPU. The **baud rate** is the **agreed-upon speaking speed** between two post offices. If the sender speaks at 9600 letters/second and the receiver listens at 4800 letters/second, the message will be unintelligible. Hence, both ends must configure **Timer 1** to produce the *exact same* timing. ## 1.3 Key Physical Constants & Standards > [!NOTE] > **Mandatory Standard Values for 8051 Serial Communication:** > - **Standard Crystal Frequency:** **11.0592 MHz** (chosen deliberately because it is an integer multiple of common baud rates, eliminating timing errors). > - **Standard Baud Rates:** **1200, 2400, 4800, 9600, 19200** bits per second. > - **Default Frame Format (Mode 1):** **1 start bit + 8 data bits + 1 stop bit** (10 bits total, no parity). > - **Timer 1 Mode:** Always **Mode 2** (8-bit auto-reload) for baud rate generation. > - **SMOD Bit (PCON.7):** Doubles the baud rate when set to **1**. --- ## 1.4 Core Register Inventory | Register | Address (Hex) | Bit-Addressable? | Primary Role | |---|---|---|---| | **SBUF** | **99H** | No | Holds the byte to be transmitted or the byte just received | | **SCON** | **98H** | **Yes** | Controls serial port mode, reception enable, and flags | | **PCON** | **87H** | No | Contains the **SMOD** bit (bit 7) for baud rate doubling | | **TMOD** | **89H** | No | Configures Timer 1 in **Mode 2** for baud rate generation | | **TH1** | **8DH** | No | Holds the auto-reload value defining the baud rate | | **TL1** | **8BH** | No | The actual timer counter (auto-reloaded from TH1) | | **IE** | **A8H** | **Yes** | Enables the Serial Port Interrupt (ES bit, IE.4) | # 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 SCON Register — The Serial Control Hub The **SCON (98H)** register is the master control block of the 8051's serial port. It is bit-addressable and reset to **00H** on power-up. | Bit | Name | Function | |---|---|---| | **7** | **SM0** | Serial Mode bit 0 | | **6** | **SM1** | Serial Mode bit 1 | | **5** | **SM2** | Multiprocessor Communication Enable (set to 0 in Mode 1 for normal use) | | **4** | **REN** | **Receive Enable** — must be set to **1** to allow reception | | **3** | **TB8** | 9th transmitted bit (used in Modes 2 & 3) | | **2** | **RB8** | 9th received bit (used in Modes 2 & 3) | | **1** | **TI** | **Transmit Interrupt Flag** — set by hardware at end of transmission; **must be cleared by software** | | **0** | **RI** | **Receive Interrupt Flag** — set by hardware at end of reception; **must be cleared by software** | ### The Four Serial Modes (SM0, SM1) | SM0 | SM1 | Mode | Description | Baud Rate Source | |---|---|---|---|---| | 0 | 0 | **Mode 0** | 8-bit Shift Register | Fixed: **Oscillator / 12** | | 0 | 1 | **Mode 1** | **8-bit UART (Standard)** | **Timer 1 Overflow (variable)** | | 1 | 0 | Mode 2 | 9-bit UART | Fixed: **Oscillator / 32** or **/64** | | 1 | 1 | Mode 3 | 9-bit UART | **Timer 1 Overflow (variable)** | > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU High-Yield Focus:** Over 95% of KTU exam problems on serial port programming use **Mode 1 (SM0=0, SM1=1)**. The standard SCON value for **transmission** is **0x40 (01000000B)** and for **reception** is **0x50 (01010000B)** — the only difference is that REN is set in the latter. ## 2.2 SBUF Register — The Dual-Buffer Architecture Physically, the 8051 contains **two separate 8-bit registers** that share the single SFR address **99H**: - **Writing** to SBUF → loads the **Transmit Buffer** (data is shifted out via TxD). - **Reading** from SBUF → reads the **Receive Buffer** (data assembled from RxD). This dual-buffer design allows **full-duplex** communication (simultaneous transmit and receive). ## 2.3 PCON Register — The SMOD Bit Only bit 7 of PCON is relevant here. When **SMOD = 1**, the baud rate is **doubled** (multiplied by 2). When **SMOD = 0** (the default after reset), the standard formula applies. ## 2.4 Timer 1 Configuration for Baud Rate Generation To generate a stable baud rate, Timer 1 must be configured in **Mode 2 (8-bit Auto-Reload)**. The steps are: 1. Set the **C/T̄** bit of TMOD to **0** (timer mode, not counter mode). 2. Set the **M1, M0** bits of TMOD to **1, 0** respectively (Mode 2). 3. Load **TH1** with the calculated reload value. 4. Start the timer by setting the **TR1** bit in the TCON register. 5. Ensure **TF1** is cleared. ## 2.5 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet > [!NOTE] > The following table contains **every formula** you need for KTU 2024 serial port numerical problems. Memorize the two boxed equations — they appear in almost every university exam question. | # | Quantity | Formula | Units / Notes | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Timer 1 Overflow Rate | $f_{ov} = \dfrac{f_{osc}}{12 \times (256 - TH1)}$ | Overflows per second (Hz) | | 2 | **Baud Rate (General)** | $\boxed{Baud = \dfrac{2^{SMOD}}{32} \times f_{ov}}$ | Bits per second (bps) | | 3 | **Baud Rate (Expanded)** | $\boxed{Baud = \dfrac{2^{SMOD} \times f_{osc}}{32 \times 12 \times (256 - TH1)}}$ | The master equation for all problems | | 4 | TH1 (SMOD = 0) | $TH1 = 256 - \dfrac{f_{osc}}{384 \times Baud}$ | Most common case | | 5 | TH1 (SMOD = 1) | $TH1 = 256 - \dfrac{f_{osc}}{192 \times Baud}$ | When baud rate doubling is used | | 6 | SMOD Bit Value | Located at **PCON.7** | 0 = Normal, 1 = Doubled | > [!WARNING] > **Markdown Rendering Note:** In the table above, the absolute value bars around $f_{ov}$ and the frequency $f_{osc}$ use the word-spelled form (\vert). When copying into handwritten KTU answer sheets, restore them to standard vertical bars $\vert \cdot \vert$. ## 2.6 Reference Table — TH1 Values for 11.0592 MHz Crystal | Baud Rate | SMOD | TH1 (Decimal) | TH1 (Hex) | Error | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1200 | 0 | 232 | **E8H** | 0% | | 2400 | 0 | 244 | **F4H** | 0% | | 4800 | 0 | 250 | **FAH** | 0% | | **9600** | 0 | 253 | **FDH** | **0%** | | 19200 | 0 | ? | ? | (Non-integer — use 1200 with SMOD=1) | ## 2.7 Real-World Engineering Utility Serial port programming is the **foundation of all embedded device communication**. It is used in: - **GPS modules** (NMEA 0183 standard, 4800 baud, 8N1). - **GSM/Bluetooth modules** (HC-05, SIM800 — 9600 baud AT-command interface). - **PC ↔ Microcontroller debugging interfaces** (Arduino bootloader, ISP programmers). - **Industrial sensor networks** (Modbus RTU protocol over RS-485). - **Inter-MCU communication** in multi-chip embedded systems. # 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Derivation of the 8051 Baud Rate Equation The 8051 baud rate is derived from the fundamental relationship between the oscillator, the timer, and the UART hardware divider. ### Step 1: Timer 1 Machine Cycle The 8051 divides the external oscillator frequency by 12 to generate the **machine cycle**, which is the basic unit of time for all on-chip timers. $$f_{machine} = \dfrac{f_{osc}}{12}$$ ### Step 2: Timer 1 Overflow Frequency In Mode 2 (8-bit auto-reload), Timer 1 counts from the value in **TH1** up to **255**, then overflows to **0** on the next pulse and reloads **TH1** automatically. The number of timer ticks per overflow is therefore: $$N_{ticks} = 256 - TH1$$ The overflow frequency is the machine cycle frequency divided by the number of ticks per overflow: $$f_{ov} = \dfrac{f_{osc}}{12 \times (256 - TH1)}$$ ### Step 3: UART Hardware Divider The 8051 UART hardware internally divides the timer overflow frequency by **32** to generate the bit-shift clock. If the **SMOD** bit is set, the divisor becomes **16** (effectively multiplying the baud rate by 2). $$Baud = \dfrac{f_{ov}}{32} \times 2^{SMOD} = \dfrac{2^{SMOD} \times f_{ov}}{32}$$ ### Step 4: Combining the Equations Substituting the expression for $f_{ov}$ from Step 2 into the equation in Step 3 yields the **master baud rate formula**: $$Baud = \dfrac{2^{SMOD} \times f_{osc}}{32 \times 12 \times (256 - TH1)}$$ > This is the single most important equation for the entire topic. Every numerical problem in KTU Module 4 reduces to manipulating this formula. ## 3.2 Worked Example 1 — Finding TH1 for 9600 Baud **Problem:** An 8051 system uses an **11.0592 MHz** crystal and requires **9600 baud** with **SMOD = 0**. Calculate the TH1 value. ### Step-by-Step Solution Given: - $f_{osc} = 11{,}059{,}200$ Hz - $Baud = 9600$ bps - $SMOD = 0 \Rightarrow 2^{SMOD} = 1$ Rearranging the master formula to solve for $(256 - TH1)$: $$256 - TH1 = \dfrac{2^{SMOD} \times f_{osc}}{32 \times 12 \times Baud}$$ Substituting numerical values: $$256 - TH1 = \dfrac{1 \times 11{,}059{,}200}{384 \times 9600}$$ Computing the denominator: $$384 \times 9600 = 3{,}686{,}400$$ Performing the division: $$256 - TH1 = \dfrac{11{,}059{,}200}{3{,}686{,}400} = 3$$ Therefore: $$TH1 = 256 - 3 = 253 = \text{FDH}$$ **Verification (error check):** $$Baud_{actual} = \dfrac{1 \times 11{,}059{,}200}{384 \times 3} = \dfrac{11{,}059{,}200}{1{,}152} = 9600 \text{ bps} \checkmark$$ **Error = 0%** — confirming why 11.0592 MHz is the universal KTU exam crystal frequency. ## 3.3 Worked Example 2 — Doubling Baud Rate with SMOD **Problem:** Same 8051 system as above, but the design now requires **19200 baud**. Find the TH1 value, assuming **SMOD = 1**. Rearranging for $(256 - TH1)$ with $2^{SMOD} = 2$: $$256 - TH1 = \dfrac{2 \times 11{,}059{,}200}{384 \times 19200}$$ Simplifying: $$256 - TH1 = \dfrac{22{,}118{,}400}{7{,}372{,}800} = 3$$ Therefore: $$TH1 = 253 = \text{FDH}$$ **Conclusion:** Setting **SMOD = 1** doubles the baud rate from 9600 to 19200 *without changing TH1*. This is a frequent KTU trick question. ## 3.4 Worked Example 3 — Finding the Resulting Baud Rate **Problem:** TH1 = 0xFA (250), $f_{osc} = 11.0592$ MHz, SMOD = 0. Calculate the baud rate. Substituting into the master formula: $$Baud = \dfrac{1 \times 11{,}059{,}200}{384 \times (256 - 250)}$$ $$Baud = \dfrac{11{,}059{,}200}{384 \times 6} = \dfrac{11{,}059{,}200}{2{,}304} = 4800 \text{ bps} \checkmark$$ ## 3.5 Analytical Matrix — Common KTU Calculation Scenarios | Scenario | Known | Find | Key Formula Inversion | |---|---|---|---| | Find TH1 | $f_{osc}$, Baud, SMOD | TH1 | $TH1 = 256 - \dfrac{2^{SMOD} \times f_{osc}}{384 \times Baud}$ | | Find Baud | $f_{osc}$, TH1, SMOD | Baud | $Baud = \dfrac{2^{SMOD} \times f_{osc}}{384 \times (256 - TH1)}$ | | Find $f_{osc}$ | TH1, Baud, SMOD | $f_{osc}$ | $f_{osc} = \dfrac{384 \times Baud \times (256 - TH1)}{2^{SMOD}}$ | | Find % Error | Computed Baud vs. Standard | Error | $Error \% = \dfrac{\vert Baud_{actual} - Baud_{ideal} \vert}{Baud_{ideal}} \times 100$ | > [!NOTE] > **Sanity Check Rule:** The value $(256 - TH1)$ must always be a **positive integer** between 1 and 255. If you obtain a non-integer, the crystal frequency cannot perfectly produce that baud rate — this is why 11.0592 MHz dominates KTU problems. ## 3.6 The Two-Flag Polling Sequence (Why TI and RI Are Not Auto-Cleared) A common KTU conceptual question is: *"Why must the programmer clear TI and RI manually?"* The answer lies in the hardware architecture: 1. When the last stop bit of a transmitted byte is shifted out, the hardware **sets TI = 1** to signal completion. 2. The hardware has **no mechanism** to clear TI because the same flag must remain set until the software has dispatched the next byte — clearing it prematurely would corrupt the next transmission. 3. The **standard practice** is to clear TI immediately after detecting it in the polling loop, *before* loading the next byte into SBUF. The identical logic applies to **RI** on the receive side. # 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Block Diagram — 8051 Internal UART Architecture The following Mermaid diagram illustrates the internal data flow of the 8051's serial port subsystem, showing the relationship between the CPU, the dual SBUF, the SCON control register, Timer 1, and the external TxD/RxD pins. ```mermaid flowchart LR cpu1[CPU CORE] sbufTx[TRANSMIT SBUF
99H Write] sbufRx[RECEIVE SBUF
99H Read] scon1[SCON REGISTER
98H SM0 SM1 REN TI RI] tmod1[TMOD REGISTER
89H Timer 1 Config] th1reg[TH1 RELOAD
8DH] tl1reg[TL1 COUNTER
8BH] tr1bit[TR1 BIT
TCON.6] pcon1[PCON.7 SMOD BIT] txd1[TXD PIN P3.1] rxd1[RXD PIN P3.0] osci1[OSCILLATOR
11.0592 MHz] div1[DIVIDE BY 12] div2[DIVIDE BY 32 OR 16] shift1[SHIFT REGISTER CLOCK] cpu1 -- write byte --> sbufTx sbufTx --> shift1 shift1 --> txd1 rxd1 --> shift1 shift1 --> sbufRx sbufRx -- read byte --> cpu1 scon1 -- controls --> shift1 scon1 -- sets TI --> cpu1 scon1 -- sets RI --> cpu1 osci1 --> div1 div1 --> tl1reg th1reg -- auto reload --> tl1reg tl1reg -- overflow --> div2 pcon1 -- selects /32 or /16 --> div2 div2 --> shift1 tr1bit -- enables --> tl1reg tmod1 -- configures --> th1reg tmod1 -- configures --> tl1reg ``` ## 4.2 Asynchronous Serial Frame Format (Mode 1) In Mode 1, every transmitted byte is encapsulated in a **10-bit frame** consisting of a start bit, eight data bits (LSB first), and a stop bit. The line idles HIGH (logic 1) between frames. ```mermaid flowchart LR A1[IDLE LINE
HIGH 1] --> B1[START BIT
LOW 0] B1 --> C1[DATA BIT D0
LSB FIRST] C1 --> D1[DATA BIT D1] D1 --> E1[DATA BIT D2] E1 --> F1[DATA BIT D3] F1 --> G1[DATA BIT D4] G1 --> H1[DATA BIT D5] H1 --> I1[DATA BIT D6] I1 --> J1[DATA BIT D7
MSB] J1 --> K1[STOP BIT
HIGH 1] K1 --> A1 ``` ## 4.3 Algorithm Flowchart — Transmitting a Byte The standard polling-based transmission sequence is captured below. The CPU writes the data byte to SBUF, then enters a busy-wait loop until the TI flag becomes 1, after which it clears TI and proceeds. ```mermaid flowchart TD stepA1[START] stepA2[Initialize SCON to 0x40
SM0 0 SM1 1 REN 0] stepA3[Configure TMOD Timer 1
in Mode 2] stepA4[Load TH1 with reload value] stepA5[Set TR1 to 1
Start Timer 1] stepA6[Load data byte into SBUF] stepA7{TI flag equals 1?} stepA8[Wait for TI to be set
by hardware at end of frame] stepA9[Clear TI flag
by software] stepA10[Transmission complete
Ready for next byte] stepA11[END] stepA1 --> stepA2 stepA2 --> stepA3 stepA3 --> stepA4 stepA4 --> stepA5 stepA5 --> stepA6 stepA6 --> stepA7 stepA7 -- NO --> stepA8 stepA8 --> stepA7 stepA7 -- YES --> stepA9 stepA9 --> stepA10 stepA10 --> stepA11 ``` ## 4.4 Algorithm Flowchart — Receiving a Byte The reception sequence is similar but with the additional requirement of enabling REN and waiting for the RI flag. The received byte is then read from SBUF and RI is cleared. ```mermaid flowchart TD stepB1[START] stepB2[Initialize SCON to 0x50
SM0 0 SM1 1 REN 1] stepB3[Configure TMOD Timer 1
in Mode 2] stepB4[Load TH1 with reload value] stepB5[Set TR1 to 1
Start Timer 1] stepB6{RI flag equals 1?} stepB7[Hardware assembles byte
in RxD and sets RI] stepB8[Read received byte
from SBUF] stepB9[Clear RI flag
by software] stepB10[Process received byte] stepB11[END] stepB1 --> stepB2 stepB2 --> stepB3 stepB3 --> stepB4 stepB4 --> stepB5 stepB5 --> stepB6 stepB6 -- NO --> stepB7 stepB7 --> stepB6 stepB6 -- YES --> stepB8 stepB8 --> stepB9 stepB9 --> stepB10 stepB10 --> stepB11 ``` ## 4.5 Complete Program — Polling-Based Transmit "A" Continuously The following 8051 assembly program transmits the ASCII character 'A' (41H) repeatedly. Each step is mapped to the flowchart in Section 4.3. ```mermaid flowchart TD p1[ORG 0000H] p2[MOV SCON 0x40] p3[MOV TMOD 0x20] p4[MOV TH1 0xFD] p5[SETB TR1] p6[MOV SBUF A] p7[WAIT: JNB TI WAIT] p8[CLR TI] p9[SJMP BACK] p1 --> p2 p2 --> p3 p3 --> p4 p4 --> p5 p5 --> p6 p6 --> p7 p7 -- TI 0 --> p7 p7 -- TI 1 --> p8 p8 --> p9 p9 --> p6 ``` | Line | Mnemonic | Comment | |---|---|---| | 1 | `MOV SCON, #40H` | Mode 1, REN = 0 (transmit only) | | 2 | `MOV TMOD, #20H` | Timer 1 in Mode 2 (auto-reload) | | 3 | `MOV TH1, #0FDH` | Reload value for 9600 baud @ 11.0592 MHz | | 4 | `SETB TR1` | Start Timer 1 | | 5 | `MOV SBUF, #'A'` | Load ASCII 'A' into transmit buffer | | 6 | `HERE: JNB TI, HERE` | Wait until TI = 1 (transmission complete) | | 7 | `CLR TI` | Clear TI for next transmission | | 8 | `SJMP BACK` | Loop back to send again | # 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) ### Question 1 [KTU University Exam — May 2024] > **Explain the role of the SCON register in 8051 serial communication. List the functions of SM0, SM1, REN, TI, and RI bits.** **Model Answer:** The **SCON (Serial Control, address 98H)** register is an 8-bit, bit-addressable Special Function Register that controls the operating mode, reception, and interrupt flags of the 8051's on-chip UART. Its five key bits perform the following roles: - **SM0, SM1 (bits 7, 6):** *Serial Mode Select* bits. Together they select one of four UART modes. The combination **SM0 = 0, SM1 = 1** selects **Mode 1**, which is the standard 8-bit variable-baud-rate UART used in virtually all KTU exam problems. - **REN (bit 4):** *Receive Enable*. Must be set to **1** by software to allow the UART to accept incoming data on the RxD pin. Cleared to 0 in transmit-only applications. - **TI (bit 1):** *Transmit Interrupt flag*. Automatically set to 1 by hardware when the last stop bit of a transmitted byte is shifted out. **Must be cleared by software** before the next transmission. - **RI (bit 0):** *Receive Interrupt flag*. Automatically set to 1 by hardware when a complete byte has been received and latched into the SBUF receive buffer. **Must be cleared by software** before the next reception is acknowledged. --- ### Question 2 [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023] > **Why is the crystal frequency 11.0592 MHz preferred over 12 MHz for 8051 serial communication?** **Model Answer:** The crystal frequency **11.0592 MHz** is preferred for 8051 serial communication because it is an **integer multiple** of all standard baud rates when divided by the standard UART hardware divisor of 384. Specifically: $$\dfrac{11{,}059{,}200}{384} = 28{,}800$$ This value is evenly divisible by 9600, 4800, 2400, and 1200, producing **exact integer TH1 reload values** (253, 250, 244, 232 respectively). In contrast, the commonly available 12 MHz crystal yields non-integer values such as TH1 = 252.745 for 9600 baud, which would have to be rounded to either 253 or 252, introducing a **baud rate error of up to 8.5%**. Such an error causes corrupted data in standard serial communication. Hence, 11.0592 MHz is the **de facto standard** for 8051 UART-based designs and is the assumed frequency in all KTU numerical problems unless stated otherwise. --- ## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each) ### KTU ESE Module Internal Choice > *(Answer ONE full question from this pair)* --- ### Question A (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam — May 2024] > **(a)** An 8051 system uses an **11.0592 MHz** crystal and needs to communicate at **2400 baud** in **Mode 1**. Calculate the required **TH1 value** for **SMOD = 0** and **SMOD = 1**. Show all derivation steps. **(7 Marks)** > > **(b)** Write a complete **8051 assembly program** to transmit the byte stored in **internal RAM location 30H** to a PC, and then continuously transmit the message **"HELLO"**. Identify the role of **pins P3.0 (RxD) and P3.1 (TxD)**, and the **internal operation of SBUF and SCON** during a single byte transmission in Mode 1. **(7 Marks)** > > **(b)** A 8051 system has $f_{osc} = 11.0592$ MHz, TH1 = 0xFD, and SMOD = 0. Calculate the **actual baud rate** and the **percentage error** with respect to the standard 9600 baud. Justify why this error is exactly 0%. **(7 Marks)** #### Model Solution — Part (a) The 8051 serial communication in **Mode 1** operates as follows: **External Pin Functions:** - **P3.0 (RxD):** *Receive Data* pin — input line for incoming serial frames from an external device (e.g., a PC's COM port or a Bluetooth module). - **P3.1 (TxD):** *Transmit Data* pin — output line that shifts out the serial frame one bit at a time at the programmed baud rate. The line idles HIGH. **Internal Operation (Step-by-Step for One Transmitted Byte):** 1. The CPU writes a data byte to **SBUF (99H)** via the `MOV SBUF, A` instruction. 2. The byte is loaded into the **transmit shift register** (one of the two physical SBUF registers). 3. The UART hardware transmits a **start bit (0)**, followed by the **8 data bits (LSB first)**, and finally a **stop bit (1)** — a total of 10 bits per frame. 4. The bit-shift clock is derived from **Timer 1's overflow rate** divided by 32 (or 16 if SMOD=1). 5. When the last stop bit is shifted out, the hardware sets the **TI flag (SCON.1) to 1**. 6. The CPU detects TI = 1 by polling (`JNB TI, $`) or via the serial interrupt vector at 0023H. 7. The CPU **clears TI by software** to prepare for the next transmission. For reception, the process is mirrored: REN must be enabled, the hardware monitors RxD for a falling edge (start bit), samples the line at the bit center for each of the 8 data bits, latches the byte into the receive SBUF, and sets RI to 1. --- #### Model Solution — Part (b) **Given:** - $f_{osc} = 11{,}059{,}200$ Hz - $TH1 = 0\text{xFD} = 253$ (decimal) - $SMOD = 0$ **Step 1: Compute $(256 - TH1)$** $$256 - 253 = 3$$ **Step 2: Apply the Baud Rate Formula** $$Baud = \dfrac{2^{SMOD} \times f_{osc}}{384 \times (256 - TH1)}$$ $$Baud = \dfrac{1 \times 11{,}059{,}200}{384 \times 3}$$ $$Baud = \dfrac{11{,}059{,}200}{1{,}152} = 9{,}600 \text{ bps}$$ **Step 3: Compute the Percentage Error** $$Error\% = \dfrac{\vert Baud_{actual} - Baud_{ideal} \vert}{Baud_{ideal}} \times 100\%$$ $$Error\% = \dfrac{\vert 9600 - 9600 \vert}{9600} \times 100\% = 0\%$$ **Justification:** The error is exactly 0% because the value $(256 - TH1) = 3$ is an **integer** that produces a clean division. This is a direct consequence of choosing the crystal frequency **11.0592 MHz**, which is the smallest integer multiple of 9600 that satisfies the 8051 hardware divider chain. Specifically: $$11{,}059{,}200 = 9600 \times 1152 = 9600 \times 384 \times 3$$ All terms divide evenly, so no fractional rounding is required. --- > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Mark-Loss Pitfalls:** > > 1. **Forgetting to clear TI/RI by software:** This is the **#1 mistake** in KTU 8051 serial port answers. **must be cleared by software**. - [ ] **Timer 1 Mode 2** (8-bit auto-reload) is mandatory for baud rate generation. - [ ] **TMOD = 0x20** configures Timer 1 in Mode 2. - [ ] **Master Baud Rate Formula:** $$Baud = \dfrac{2^{SMOD} \times f_{osc}}{384 \times (256 - TH1)}$$ - [ ] **TH1 Quick Reference (11.0592 MHz, SMOD=0):** 9600 → 0xFD, 4800 → 0xFA, 2400 → 0xF4, 1200 → 0xE8. - [ ] **SMOD bit is PCON.7**;
